entries.title: Axial Seamount
paragraphs: Axial Seamount is a basaltic submarine volcano about 480 km off the Oregon coast, sitting where the Cobb hotspot passes beneath the Juan de Fuca Ridge. That combination -- a hotspot's steady magma supply layered onto a spreading ridge -- makes it the most active, most closely watched submarine volcano in the northeast Pacific.

Its summit holds an unusually shaped rectangular caldera, about 3 km by 8 km, bounded by faults with as much as 150 m of relief; the caldera floor is roughly 50 m deeper on its north side than its south. The shallowest point on this tile, 1,395 m, sits on that summit high, close to the 1,410 m summit depth published for the volcano.

Axial has erupted at least three times since routine monitoring began: January 1998, April 2011 and April 2015. Each event is tracked by seafloor pressure and tilt instruments that catch the volcano visibly deflating as magma drains out beneath it, then slowly re-inflating over the following years -- the basis for the eruption forecasts described later in this guide.

facts.label: Summit depth
facts.value: about 1,410 m (published); 1,395 m on this tile

entries.title: Mushroom and Inferno
paragraphs: The ASHES (Axial Seamount Hydrothermal Emissions Study) vent field sits near the base of the caldera's western wall, at about 1,540-1,552 m, and has been studied since it was first surveyed in the late 1980s. Its two best-known chimneys, Mushroom and Inferno, sit roughly 10 m apart.

Mushroom is a roughly 4 m sulfide chimney with several discharge points. OOI footage shows clear flow as well as small active black-smoker chimlets, so one chimney can carry more than one kind of discharge. The cabled observatory’s HD camera watches the chimney and the animals around it.

Inferno vents high-temperature fluid too and hosts one of the densest clusters of animals at ASHES: tube worms and palm worms cling directly to its metal-sulfide-rich walls, tolerant of both scalding vent fluid and near-freezing seawater within centimetres of each other.
The compact field occupies about 2,826 square metres, roughly the area of one 43 × 61 m terrain cell. Its individual chimneys need much finer mapping to resolve.
The sulfide mound with its cluster of smokers, tubeworms and bacterial mats beside Inferno is a game addition, modelled on how chimneys group on real ASHES mounds.

entries.title: Hell, Phoenix, Virgin and Virgin Mound
paragraphs: ASHES holds several smaller sulfide structures beyond Mushroom and Inferno, all generally under 4 m tall with multiple narrow discharge orifices: Hell, Phoenix and Virgin. A separate, much smaller feature, Virgin Mound, is a sub-metre anhydrite spire venting some of the most CO2-rich fluid found anywhere in the caldera.
None of these has a published coordinate or height beyond 'less than about 4 m.'

entries.title: Life on the chimneys
paragraphs: ASHES supports a dense community built entirely on chemosynthesis: bacteria that oxidise hydrogen sulfide from the vent fluid form the base of a food web with no sunlight at all. Ridgeia tube worms, palm worms and sulfide worms crowd the warmest chimney surfaces, while limpets and scale worms graze among them and spider crabs pick through the debris.

Filamentous bacterial mats and lavender-blue ciliate protists coat rock surfaces near diffuse, lower-temperature flow. Notably, the large clams common at many black-smoker fields are absent from ASHES's chimney faces -- they turn up instead at the field's diffuse-flow sites, away from the hottest fluid.

entries.title: The caldera's western wall
paragraphs: ASHES sits close to the base of the caldera's western boundary fault, the scarp that marks the edge of the collapsed summit. On this tile's real bathymetry, the seabed rises steadily from about 1,540 m at the vent field to around 1,416 m only 300 m to the west, consistent with the toe of that wall.

The fault trace itself -- described in the literature as roughly 130 m west of ASHES -- is finer than this tile's ~43 x 61 m grid cells can resolve individually, so this POI marks the real, surveyed rising terrain rather than a specific fault line.

entries.title: A resurfaced caldera floor
paragraphs: Axial's caldera floor has been repeatedly paved over by lava from its recorded eruptions: a 1998 flow up to 13 m thick, a 2011 flow roughly three times larger, and a further flow in 2015, the first submarine eruption ever recorded live by a seafloor cabled observatory.

This POI sits on a broad, shallow rise on the caldera floor south of ASHES, about 1,460 m deep against roughly 1,530-1,540 m on the surrounding floor -- the kind of low, hummocky high left behind by a lava flow. No source maps this specific rise to one dated eruption, so it is described here as caldera-floor lava terrain in general rather than attributed to a single flow.

entries.title: Forecasting the next eruption
paragraphs: Axial Seamount inflates like a slow-filling balloon between eruptions as magma accumulates beneath the caldera, then deflates abruptly when an eruption drains that reservoir -- 3.2 m of sudden subsidence in 1998, 2.4 m in 2011. Bill Chadwick (Oregon State University / NOAA PMEL) and Scott Nooner (University of North Carolina Wilmington) noticed this repeating pattern and, in September 2014, used it to forecast the 2015 eruption about seven months before it happened -- the first successful forecast of a submarine volcanic eruption.
Pressure sensors, tiltmeters and earthquake recordings let scientists follow the volcano as it refills. An eruption forecast changes as those measurements change; inflation alone is not a countdown.

facts.label: Status as of Sept. 2026
facts.value: fully re-inflated; low seismicity; no eruption imminent

entries.title: The caldera rim and cabled observatory
paragraphs: The shallowest terrain on this tile, 1,395 m, sits on the caldera's summit high about 1.4 km north-east of the ASHES chimneys -- close to the 1,410 m summit depth published for the volcano, given this grid's resolution. It marks the top of the rectangular caldera whose bounding faults drop as much as 150 m to the floor.

Axial is wired for real-time science: the Ocean Observatories Initiative's Regional Cabled Array, run by the University of Washington, threads hundreds of kilometres of fibre-optic cable across the seamount to more than a dozen instrument sites, including ASHES, streaming live seismic, pressure, temperature, chemistry and HD video data to shore continuously. It is one of the only deep hydrothermal systems on Earth monitored this way, which is what makes eruption forecasts like the one above possible at all.
